analysis.one_liner: Lets workers in employer health plans appeal denied care to outside experts and sue for damages.
analysis.headline: The bill was assigned to a House subcommittee in September 1999, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the federal law that governs most employer-provided health plans. Health plans would have to give written reasons for denying care, decide routine claims within 14 days and emergency claims within 72 hours, and let patients appeal denials to a physician who wasn't involved in the first decision, then to an outside independent expert. It would also let patients sue a plan for damages when careless denial of care causes injury or death — something federal law generally blocks today.
analysis.who_benefits: People insured through their employer's health plan — the majority of working-age Americans with private coverage — who are denied a treatment or payment. They would get faster answers, a genuinely independent outside review of denials, and a real courtroom remedy when a wrongful denial causes injury or death.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to give written, understandable notice of any denial — to the patient and the treating doctor — stating the specific reasons and the patient's appeal rights.
Sets deadlines: plans must decide routine claims within 14 days and emergency-care requests within 72 hours, and complete internal appeals on the same clocks.
Requires that appeals over medical necessity or 'experimental treatment' denials be reviewed by a qualified physician who did not make the original denial.

Gives patients access to external review by independent medical experts, chosen through a process designed to hide their identities from both the plan and the patient; the experts' decision becomes the plan's final decision.

Creates a federal cause of action letting a patient recover actual damages — including compensatory and consequential damages — from a plan fiduciary whose failure to exercise ordinary care in denying coverage causes personal injury or wrongful death, with expedited court access when a physician certifies that waiting for appeals risks irreparable harm to health.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed-care plans, which would face review deadlines, outside reviews, and damage awards for careless denials, and would likely pass some of that cost to employers and plan sponsors through premiums.

drawbacks.text: Punitive damages are tightly limited: they are allowed only for 'conscious, flagrant indifference' proven by clear and convincing evidence, capped at the greater of twice economic losses or $250,000, with the court rather than the jury managing the cap.
The bill preempts similar state-law damage actions, which could replace stronger remedies some states already provide patients with this federal floor.
Patients must exhaust all internal appeals and external review before suing, and the bill presumes the outside expert's decision is correct — a heavy gate before any courtroom remedy.

Employers and plan sponsors are exempt from liability unless they directly made the final claim decision themselves, and the whole framework has a sunset: it lapses for plan years beginning January 1, 2005.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are real and directly aimed at the biggest gap in employer-plan coverage — federal law's near-total bar on suing for wrongly denied care. But the bill is deliberately modest: tight damage caps, a mandatory review gauntlet before suing, a shield for employers, and a five-year sunset. It reads as a middle path in the era's 'patients' bill of rights' fight — more than patients had, less than full state-court remedies — and it may have undercut stronger alternatives by preempting them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Van Hilleary introduced the bill on August 5, 1999, for himself and Rep. Jo Ann Emerson; it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
On September 10, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations — the panel that handles ERISA health-plan issues.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The bill died in subcommittee when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers offering ERISA-covered plans, who kept the federal shield that blocks patients from recovering damages for wrongly denied care, and the committee leaders who never had to take a position on it.

for.name: Rep. Van Hilleary
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to add appeal procedures and court remedies to ERISA group health plans.

for.name: Rep. Jo Ann Emerson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only additional supporter.

against.name: John Boehner
against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his subcommittee on September 10, 1999, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled; it died there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was written and sponsored by two Republicans, but it never reached a vote, so the record shows no party split on it; it simply died in a Republican-run subcommittee.

industries.note: The bill would end their practical immunity from damages suits over wrongly denied care and impose hard deadlines and independent review of denials. Their cost of doing business rises; patients get enforceable rights.

The bill explicitly shields employers from lawsuits unless they personally made the final claim decision, but they could still face higher premiums as insurers price in liability. The shield is a carve-out the insurance-friendly structure of the bill traded for employer support.

industries.industry: Independent medical review and external review organizations
industries.note: The bill creates a mandatory external review step using independent medical and contract experts selected under independence rules — new paid work for accreditation bodies, review organizations, and physician panels.
